questions.question: A probability line has five labels in order from left to right: impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, certain. A spinner is divided into 4 equal parts, and all 4 parts are coloured red. Where on the probability line does the outcome ‘the arrow lands on red’ belong?
options: At certain
At likely
At unlikely
At impossible
questions.explain: Every one of the 4 equal parts is red, so the arrow must land on red — that is the certain end of the line. A common trap is choosing likely; likely means it will probably happen, but certain means there is no other way it can turn out.

questions.question: A probability line has five labels in order from left to right: impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, certain. A spinner is divided into 8 equal parts: 4 parts are blue and 4 parts are yellow. Where does the outcome ‘the arrow lands on blue’ belong?
options: At the far right end, at certain
Right in the middle, at equally likely
At the far left end, at impossible
Between impossible and equally likely, at unlikely
questions.explain: There are 4 blue parts and 4 yellow parts out of 8 equal parts, so blue and yellow have the same chance and the outcome sits in the middle at equally likely. Many students slide toward likely just because 4 sounds like a lot — compare the two colours instead of looking at one number alone.

questions.question: A probability line has five labels in order from left to right: impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, certain. A spinner is divided into 10 equal parts: 1 part is green and the other 9 parts are white. Where does the outcome ‘the arrow lands on green’ belong?
options: At the far left end, at impossible
Right in the middle, at equally likely
Just to the right of impossible, at unlikely
At the far right end, at certain
questions.explain: Only 1 of the 10 equal parts is green, so landing on green can happen but probably will not — that is unlikely. The usual mistake is jumping all the way to impossible; impossible means the outcome can never happen, and green is on the spinner.

questions.question: A probability line has five labels in order from left to right: impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, certain. A spinner is divided into 6 equal parts: 5 parts are orange and 1 part is white. Where does the outcome ‘the arrow lands on orange’ belong?
options: Right in the middle, at equally likely
At the far left end, at impossible
At the far right end, at certain
Between equally likely and certain, at likely
questions.explain: Orange covers 5 of the 6 equal parts, which is more than half but not all, so the outcome is likely. Watch the trap of saying certain — one white part is still there, so orange is not guaranteed.

questions.question: A jar in Ms. Patel's Grade 4 classroom holds 12 counters: 11 are green and 1 is white. Sofia will take one counter without looking. Which word best describes taking a green counter?
options: Likely
Equally likely
Impossible
Certain
questions.explain: Green fills 11 of the 12 counters — much more than half but not all — so taking green is likely. The most common slip is saying certain, but the single white counter means green is not guaranteed.

questions.question: Liam is rolling a number cube with the faces labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. Which outcome is impossible?
options: Rolling a 6
Rolling a number greater than 6
Rolling an odd number
Rolling a number less than 3
questions.explain: No face is larger than 6, so that outcome can never happen and it is impossible. Rolling a 6 only happens on 1 of the 6 faces, which makes it unlikely — unlikely still means it can happen, so it is not the same as impossible.

questions.question: Ms. Chan wants a spinner for a class game where landing on red is unlikely, but still possible. Every spinner below has 10 equal parts. Which spinner should she choose?
options: A spinner with 5 red parts and 5 blue parts
A spinner with 9 red parts and 1 blue part
A spinner with 1 red part and 9 blue parts
A spinner with 0 red parts and 10 blue parts
questions.explain: Unlikely but possible means red must be there but must cover much less than half, so 1 red part out of 10 equal parts is the right choice. The spinner with no red at all makes red impossible, not unlikely — those two words are not the same.

questions.question: The school store keeps 15 pencils in a cup: 5 blue, 5 red, and 5 green. Ravi takes one pencil without looking. Which statement is true?
options: Blue is certain, because blue pencils are in the cup
Green is unlikely, because it is named last
Blue is likely, because 5 pencils is a lot
Blue, red, and green are all equally likely
questions.explain: The three colours have the same number of pencils, 5 each, so no colour has a better chance and all three are equally likely. A common trap is thinking 5 is a big number and calling one colour likely — likelihood comes from comparing the colours to each other, not from one number by itself.

questions.question: A bag holds 2 red cubes and 8 blue cubes. Maya says, ‘Pulling red and pulling blue are equally likely, because there are only two colours in the bag.’ Why is Maya wrong?
options: Equally likely means the same number of each colour, and there are 8 blue but only 2 red, so blue is likely and red is unlikely
Equally likely means only one colour is in the bag, so pulling red is impossible
Pulling red is certain, because there are red cubes in the bag
She is right — with two colours, each colour gets one of the two chances
questions.explain: Equally likely depends on the amounts, not on how many colours there are: with 8 blue and only 2 red, blue is likely and red is unlikely. The classic misconception is thinking two choices always means a fair fifty-fifty chance.

questions.question: For a probability experiment, Jaya uses two spinners. Spinner A has 8 equal parts, 6 of them green. Spinner B has 4 equal parts, 2 of them green. Which statement is true?
options: Green is likely on both spinners, because both have green parts
Green is likely on Spinner A and equally likely on Spinner B
Green is equally likely on Spinner A and certain on Spinner B
Green is certain on Spinner A, because 6 is more than half of 8
questions.explain: On Spinner A, 6 of 8 equal parts are green, which is more than half, so green is likely; on Spinner B, 2 of 4 parts are green, exactly half, so green is equally likely. Do not let the bigger number of green parts push you to certain — certain would need every part to be green.

questions.question: Ravi's spinner has 5 equal parts: 1 part is blue and 4 parts are white. He spins it 20 times and his tally shows blue 6 times. Which statement is true?
options: Blue is now likely, because it came up 6 times
Blue and white are equally likely, because both colours came up in the tally
Landing on blue is still unlikely, because only 1 of the 5 equal parts is blue
Landing on blue is now certain, because blue has already happened
questions.explain: Likelihood comes from the equal parts on the spinner: 1 blue part out of 5 keeps blue unlikely, even though a few blue spins showed up in 20 tries. The common misconception is letting the tally results rewrite the spinner — real results wobble around what you expect without changing it.

questions.question: At a Burnaby soccer practice the cooler holds 4 apple juice boxes and 4 orange juice boxes, so grabbing either flavour without looking is equally likely. The coach then adds 8 more apple juice boxes to the same cooler. Which word now describes grabbing an orange juice box?
options: Impossible
Certain
Still equally likely
Unlikely
questions.explain: After the coach adds 8 apple, the cooler has 12 apple and 4 orange out of 16 boxes, so orange is far less than half and grabbing orange is unlikely. Two traps here: saying it stays equally likely because both flavours are still in there, and saying impossible even though 4 orange boxes remain.
